name: Pedro Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Whatever you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a flatbed with a crane on the back for a builders' merchant, so timber, plasterboard, bags of cement, out to building sites. I'm in the yard at half six, the loaders put it on, and I'm usually on site by eight with a foreman shouting at me about where to drop it. The crane is the part I love, swinging a pallet over a fence onto the exact spot. The part that wears me out is muddy sites where I've got to work out how to get in without sinking the wheels.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Just under a year and a half. I was in a warehouse before, picking orders, and I did my licence because the money's much better. I'm still slow with the crane controls, the older drivers do in ten minutes what takes me twenty. My partner Sofia is a nurse, so between her shifts and mine we've got decent money and we've saved about ten months' worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, the hype people can go home. On the group chat with the other drivers I'd probably post a meme about the robot that was supposed to take our jobs. Then I'd moan about diesel prices like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my plan carries on. I get quicker on the crane, I get a few more years in, and I'm on good money with Sofia's wage too. The only things on my mind would be the muddy sites and my back, because lifting the straps and chains all day isn't nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and ask Dev, the yard foreman, to put me with the senior drivers more so I learn the crane faster. I'd keep using the chatbot sometimes for things like checking load rules. And we'd keep saving toward a flat of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned using a chatbot for load rules. How does that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask it something like how heavy can a pallet be on this outrigger setting, and then I check it against the chart in the cab anyway. It's handy for the boring stuff. I wouldn't trust a chatbot with a pallet over a kid's paddling pool in someone's garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets in the way of your plan in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, really, and the hours. Sofia does nights sometimes and we only see each other at weekends then. If I'm still doing six-thirty starts at forty, I'll be falling apart, so I'd want to move into something with the crane that's less driving.

say: I'd say the **hype people** got it wrong and post a **meme** about it.
I'd go back to moaning about **diesel prices** with the other drivers.
think: My plan carries on: get **quicker on the crane** and build experience.
My real worries are **muddy sites** and my **back** from lifting chains.
do: Ask the yard foreman to pair me with **senior drivers** for crane practice.
Keep using a **chatbot** now and then to check load rules.
Keep **saving** toward a flat of our own.
S0.quote: I wouldn't trust a chatbot with a pallet over a kid's paddling pool in someone's garden.
fieldNote: He uses **AI lightly** and always checks it against the chart in the cab.
His long-term worry is **physical wear**, not technology.
Two decent wages and **ten months** saved make him feel secure.

steps.text: Ride along with senior drivers to get faster on the crane
Keep saving toward a deposit on a flat with his partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots are a long way off from swinging a crane onto a building site, so I'm not worried. But I'd also say the union should be in the room when they bring the new systems in. Workers shouldn't just get told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the office side would change a lot. The ordering, the delivery booking, the route plan, all that's software now. I'd probably get a tablet telling me my drops, which is fine, but it might also squeeze the timings so I can't take the extra ten minutes on a tricky site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the planning app properly once the others do, not before. I'd book my full crane operator ticket this year, which costs about eight hundred, so I'm more than just a driver. And I'd go to one union meeting, since I've only been a member on paper so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, I'd say. Not scared, just watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the yard would feel it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lads in the trade counter, taking phone orders, and the woman who books the deliveries. A builder could just order on a screen and pick a slot. I'd feel bad for them, because they're the ones who sort out the mess when a builder's address is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the crane ticket now, rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a driver who can only drive is the easiest thing to swap out, either for another driver or for a robot one day. If I can run the crane, I'm the person on site making decisions about where the load goes. That feels like the safer seat.

say: I'd say robots are **far from** swinging a crane on a building site.
I'd say the **union** must be in the room when new systems arrive.
think: The **office side** of ordering, booking and routing would change a lot.
A planning app might **squeeze timings** on tricky sites.
do: Start using the **planning app** once other drivers do.
Book the full **crane ticket** this year for about **eight hundred**.
Attend a **union meeting** for the first time.
S1.quote: A driver who can only drive is the easiest thing to swap out, either for another driver or for a robot one day.
fieldNote: He spots that **office tasks** go first and worries for trade counter staff.
He sees the **crane ticket** as moving from driver to decision-maker on site.
His steady streak shows: he'll adopt the app only **after others** do.

steps.text: Pay about eight hundred for the full crane operator ticket
Start using the delivery planning app once other drivers do
Go to his first union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to cope with, and the government has to slow it down or catch people. I'd be posting about a jobs guarantee or some kind of income for people pushed out. At the yard I'd tell people to join the union while it still counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think 2028 kills the office and 2031 kills the driving, but building sites are messy. A robot that drives on the motorway is one thing, a robot that finds the right fence in a muddy field and swings a pallet over it is harder. So I might have a few extra years, but I don't know that, nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the crane ticket done fast and look at becoming a slinger-signaller too, the person who guides crane loads on site. I'd keep the savings and stop eating out so much. Sofia's job in a hospital feels safer than mine, so we'd lean on that if it comes to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be thirty when the robots come, which is young to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking work goes in 2028 and hands-on work about three years later. Where does that leave your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My day is mostly hands-on, so I'd have the three years. But the bit that tells me where to go and when would be AI from day one. I'd be a pair of hands and eyes for a computer, which honestly might not be that different from now with a bossy foreman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sofia talk about at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether to buy the flat now or wait. If my wage might go in three years, a mortgage on two wages is risky. I think my partner and I would still buy a flat, but something smaller, so her nurse's pay alone could cover the mortgage.

say: I'd say this is **too fast** and the government must slow it or **catch people**.
I'd post about a **jobs guarantee** or income support for those pushed out.
think: The **office goes in 2028** and the driving around 2031.
**Muddy sites** and crane drops might buy me **extra years**, though nobody knows.
do: Finish the **crane ticket** fast and add **slinger-signaller** training.
Cut back on **eating out** and protect savings.
Lean on my partner's **hospital job** if my wage goes.
feel: **Anxious**, because thirty feels **young** to start over.
S2.quote: My partner and I would still buy a flat, but something smaller, so her nurse's pay alone could cover the mortgage.
fieldNote: He reasons carefully that **messy sites** are harder for robots than motorways.
He'd become **hands for a computer**, and jokes it's like a bossy foreman.
The **flat purchase** is where the risk lands, and he'd shrink it.

steps.text: Finish the crane ticket and add slinger-signaller training
Stop eating out most weeknights to protect savings
Buy a smaller flat that his partner's pay alone can cover
Back campaigns for a jobs guarantee for pushed-out workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the government and companies to sort out retraining if they actually want to. I'd be on at the union to get a deal with the merchant now, while they still need us. Online I'd say less and do more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's 2031 for the office and maybe 2034 for the truck. I'd be thirty-three, still young enough to switch. I think the crane gets me further than the driving, but I'd want a skill that lasts past robots altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the crane ticket this year, then start an evening course in something like electrical work in year two, because building sites still need wiring. I'd keep saving, maybe less hard. I'd also try the planning app early this time, once a couple of the drivers say it's alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the kind where you've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia's brother is an electrician and he's never short of work. Robots might pull cables one day, but finding the fault in an old house full of rubbish wiring is a puzzle that robots won't solve soon. I'd still use the crane while I trained, so there's no gap in pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the yard in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I reckon the trade counter shrinks to two people and the bookings all go online by 2031. Then the merchant starts testing self-driving trucks for the simple drops, the ones to the big sites with proper roads. The tight, muddy jobs stay with us till the end.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to sort **retraining**, if they want to.
I'd push the **union** for a deal while the merchant still needs us.
think: The office goes in **2031** and the truck around **2034**, when I'm thirty-three.
The crane gets me further, but I want a **skill** that outlasts robots.
do: Start an **evening electrical course** in year two while still driving.
Try the **planning app** early once a couple of drivers approve.
S3.quote: Finding the fault in an old house full of rubbish wiring is a puzzle that robots won't solve soon.
fieldNote: More time turns his worry into a **two-step plan**: crane now, wiring later.
His partner's **brother** gives him a real model for the next trade.
He predicts **simple big-site drops** get automated before muddy ones.

steps.text: Finish the crane ticket in the first year
Start an evening electrical course in year two
Push the union for a transition deal with the merchant
Try the planning app once two drivers say it works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, so let's not waste it arguing. I'd tell people at the yard to start learning something now, slowly. And I'd say the government should pay for training for anyone whose job is on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be thirty-eight in 2039, with a crane ticket and probably a second trade. The office stuff changes around 2036, and by then I'd have moved on from just driving anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd just do the crane ticket and keep saving. In a few years I'd start the electrical course, once I see how the self-driving trucks are going. I'd buy the flat with Sofia without worrying too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for the older drivers, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said older drivers. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a driver called Paul who's fifty-five and taught me the crane. By 2039 he's retired anyway, but the ones in their forties would be stuck in the middle. I'd want the union to fight for them more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a few years before the electrical course. Isn't that leaving it late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I don't want to jump at something that might not happen. If by 2030 the self-driving trucks are working in the rain, I'll start the electrical course. That's how I do things, I wait till it's proven, then I move.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift if we stop arguing and use it.
I'd say the government should pay for **training** for any job at risk.
think: I'd be **thirty-eight** in 2039, likely with a **second trade**.
By the time office work changes, I'd have moved past **just driving**.
do: Do the **crane ticket** this year and keep saving.
Start the **electrical course** once self-driving trucks prove themselves.
Buy the **flat** with my partner without much worry.
S4.quote: If by 2030 the self-driving trucks are working in the rain, I'll start the electrical course.
fieldNote: He is **secure** himself and turns his concern to drivers in their **forties**.
He waits for **proof** before moving, true to his steady style.
He sets a clear **trigger** for acting: trucks that cope with rain.

steps.text: Get the crane operator ticket in the first year
Keep saving about the same each month
Buy a flat with his partner on two wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do anything properly, and Sofia and I would be making big decisions in a rush. What would help is free training for trades like crane work and wiring, and some kind of income for people while they retrain, so you don't have to choose between rent and a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about safety. If they put self-driving trucks on building sites, someone's going to get hurt before they get it right, and it'll probably be a labourer. I'd want rules on that before anything else.

headlineQuote: If they put self-driving trucks on building sites, someone's going to get hurt before they get it right, and it'll probably be a labourer.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old** crane-truck driver for a builders' merchant, still slow on the **crane controls**.
He and his nurse partner have about **ten months** saved and plan to buy a flat.
He uses **AI now and then** but always checks it, and adopts tools once others do.
His answer in every picture is to climb from driver to **crane operator**, then maybe **electrician**.
He stays **calm to anxious**, worrying more for older drivers and labourers than himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would force rushed decisions about the **flat** and his career.
whatWouldHelp: **Free training** in trades like crane work and wiring.
**Income support** during retraining, plus **safety rules** before self-driving trucks reach sites.
